results.title: After his 99 Cents Only Store takeover, street artist Barry McGee takes over a gallery
highlights:
[After his 99 Cents Only Store takeover, street artist Barry McGee takes over a gallery]

The tagger-turned-blue-chip artist Barry McGee reopened a former 99 Cents Only on Wilshire Boulevard for a one-week art fair event.

…

McGee and Bay Area artist Tom Franco worked with Deitch and the Hole, a gallery that has since closed its Los Angeles location, to stage the exhibition. McGee’s devoted following came out in force: Deitch estimated that about 25,000 people visited. “L.A. really showed up for that,” McGee said.

The event also drew complaints. Several neighboring businesses and apartment buildings were tagged, though McGee said the graffiti was cleaned up. In July, L.A. Taco found that several participating artists had not been paid for work sold during the exhibition. Kathy Grayson, who runs the Hole in New York, wrote in an email that all artists and vendors have since been paid. “It was a gigantic undertaking,” she wrote of staging the exhibit, adding that she had stepped in to help McGee realize his “dream-come-true project.”

…

highlights:
[U.S. Galleries and Art Spaces Shut Their Doors to Protest ICE > Sign Up For Our Daily Newsletter]

Today (Jan. 30), however, something shifted, and galleries across the U.S. have suspended operations to jointly participate in a nationwide general strike opposing the expansion of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) funding and operations. Included among them are industry heavyweights such as Gagosian, Pace Gallery, White Cube, David Zwirner, Hauser & Wirth, Lisson, Almine Rech and Perrotin, with historically significant and medium-sized spaces like Sean Kelly, Sprüth Magers, Marian Goodman, Galerie Lelong, Greene Naftali, Paula Cooper, Olney Gleason, Tanya Bonakdar, Mendes Wood DM, PPOW, Vielmetter, Shrine, Chris Sharp, Half Gallery, LATITUDE, Charles Moffett, Swivel Gallery, Margot Samel, Management and Hesse Flatow. Some institutions are also participating in the general strike, including the Drawing Center and El Museo del Barrio in New York, the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles and the Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles. They join other institutions in Minneapolis-St. Paul, including the Minneapolis Institute of Art (MIA) and the Walker Art Cent…[truncated]

results.title: NYC Selected Gallery Guide, November 2026
highlights:
[NYC Selected Gallery Guide, November 2026]

November settles in with a full roster and I’m up for it. In Tribeca, Klaus von Nichtssagend presents Tamara Gonzales, Bortolami has Rebecca Morris, who is looking kind of rosy in the preview image. Is she finally embracing a more traditional form of beauty? We’ll see. At CANADA, Xylor Jane is back with “Paintings for People.” Down on the Lower East Side, Shrine is showing Loren Erdrich while Post Times has a Fergus Feehily show, which seems like a perfect match. In Chelsea, Petzel presents Tschabalala Self, and Nicola Vassell Gallery has LIC pal Pam Glick, who says she never could have made this body of work if she hadn’t moved back to NYC. Julie Curtiss is having her first show at (gasp) Gagosian, and Eric Fischl is back with another solo at Skarstedt. Jason Stopa continues his exploration of brightly-colored architectural forms at Morgan Lehman, and Sherrie Levine is at Galerie Buchholz. If you find yourself in DUMBO, please stop by Springs Projects, 20 Jay Street, Suite 311B, to see “On Certain Grounds,” my show with Cate Holt. The opening is Thursday, November 5, 6-8 pm. I’d love to see you. – *Sharon Butler*

Also on the must-see list this month is “The Moment and the Distance,” a big Helen Frankenthaler solo at Gagosian, opening as I write this, which, with the Frankenthaler Foundation, is presenting 20 of Frankenthaler’s largest and, per Gagosian, most ambitious works. I’d think twice about calling her work “lyrical” – the recent exhibition in MoMA’s atrium proved it’s more idiosyncratic and formidable than that pretty adjective suggests. White Cube is presenting a two-person exhibition with David Hammons and Jannis Kounellis (1936–2017).
